title: The Fern That Waits for Rain

blocks.text: This is a fern. A fern is a green plant. It likes rain. It likes shade. A new fern leaf is rolled up tight. It looks like a curl. When the rain comes, the curl opens. blocks.prompt: The Dust Under the Leaf
blocks.text: A fern does not grow flowers. It does not grow seeds. So how does it make more ferns? It makes dust. The dust is called spores. Spores hide in tiny brown dots under the leaf. Turn a frond over and you can see them. When the dots are ready, they pop open. The spores blow away in the wind. If a spore lands in a wet, shady spot, a new fern can start. That is why you find ferns by streams and under big trees. Ferns need the rain. Without it, no new ferns grow.

blocks.prompt: The Plant That Cannot Grow Without Rain
blocks.text: Every plant you know has a plan for making more of itself. An apple tree makes apples with seeds inside. A dandelion makes fluff that floats. A fern does neither. A fern makes spores. Spores are so small that a cloud of them looks like a puff of smoke. They grow in clusters of brown dots on the underside of the frond. Each dot holds hundreds of them. On a dry, warm day the dots crack open and flick the spores into the air. Here is the strange part. A spore does not grow into a fern. It grows into a tiny green heart, flat as a scale and no bigger than your fingernail. That little heart makes the cells that join together to start a real fern. But those cells have to swim to meet, and they can only swim in water. A film of rain on the ground is enough. No rain, no swimming, no new fern. So a fern is not just a plant that likes wet places. It is a plant that cannot make a family without them.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Resurrection fern grows on oak branches, not in soil
It can lose most of its water and live
It turns green again a few hours after rain
An epiphyte sits on another plant

blocks.prompt: The Plant That Plays Dead
blocks.text: Walk through an oak forest in Georgia after a long dry spell and you may pass a branch covered in what looks like gray litter. The leaves are curled inward, brittle, and the color of old paper. Anyone would call them dead. They are not. That is resurrection fern, and it is waiting. Most plants die when they lose more than about a tenth of their water. Resurrection fern can lose most of the water in its body, shrivel to a husk, and stay that way for months. Then rain falls. Within a few hours the fronds uncurl, swell, and turn green again, as if someone had pressed rewind. The fern was never dead. It was shut down. It can do this because of where it lives. Resurrection fern is an epiphyte, which means it grows on other plants rather than in soil. It perches on oak limbs, high above the ground, taking nothing from the tree but a place to sit. Up there, there is no deep soil holding a reserve of moisture. The branch is wet when it rains and bone dry when it does not. A plant living in that spot has two choices: find a way to store water, or find a way to do without it. The fern does without. Every fern is tied to water, because a fern needs a film of rain to reproduce. The resurrection fern simply took the connection further. It does not fight the weather. It follows it.

a branch has no deep soil, so it is wet only when it rains and dry the rest of the time
dead means it cannot come back; shut down means it paused and can start again when water returns
(inference: instead of storing water to survive dry spells, it matches its life to whether rain is falling)

blocks.prompt: The Fern Spike
blocks.text: Everywhere on Earth there is a thin line of clay that marks the worst day in the history of animals. It sits about 66 million years ago, and geologists call it the K-Pg boundary. Below the line, rock records a world of dinosaurs. Above it, they are gone. The line itself is the dust of an asteroid roughly six miles wide that struck what is now the Yucatan coast of Mexico, throwing enough debris into the sky to dim the sun and stall photosynthesis across the planet. The interesting part, for a plant scientist, is what sits directly above the clay. If you drill a core through the boundary and count the microscopic grains preserved in each layer, you find something consistent. Below the line: pollen, in enormous variety, from a forested world. In the layer just above: almost no pollen at all, and instead a sudden flood of fern spores. In some cores, the spores make up nearly all of the material. The pattern is common enough that it has a name. Paleobotanists call it the fern spike. It is not that ferns survived the impact better than everything else. It is that ferns are first responders. A fern spore is light enough to travel for hundreds of miles on the wind, and a fern needs no partner, no pollinator, and no established soil to begin. Drop a spore on scorched, bare, damp ground and it can start. Trees cannot do that. A forest needs decades and a seed bank and animals to move the seeds around, and after the impact those things were gone. So for a stretch of years after the sky went dark, wide sections of the planet were green with almost nothing but ferns. The same thing happens on a smaller scale today. After a landslide, a wildfire, or a fresh lava flow cools, ferns are often the first green things back. The fern spike is not a story about a plant getting lucky. It is a record, written in spores, of what a broken world reaches for first.

meta.templateLabel: The Fern That Waits for Rain

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Ferns have existed for roughly 360 million years
Alternation of generations: a spore grows a separate plant
The sperm must swim through water to reach the egg
Fern spike: spores flood the layer above the asteroid clay
Azolla event: an Arctic fern bloom that buried carbon
About 10,000 fern species are alive today

blocks.prompt: Ferns and the Weather They Made
blocks.text: A fern is easy to underestimate. It has no flower to advertise itself, no fruit, no seed, and no obvious ambition. It sits in the shade being green. But ferns have been on this planet for something like 360 million years, which means they were already old when the first dinosaur appeared, and they have twice been caught in the act of doing something enormous. Start with what a fern actually is, because the strangeness begins there. The leafy plant you recognize is only half of the organism. It produces spores, and a spore does not grow into another leafy fern. It grows into a separate, independent plant, a green flake about the size of a lentil, which most people would never notice underfoot. That flake makes egg and sperm. The sperm has to swim, physically swim, across a film of water to reach the egg. Only then does the fertilized cell grow into the leafy fern we know. Biologists call the arrangement alternation of generations, and its consequence is simple and absolute: no water, no next generation. Every fern on Earth is a hostage to rainfall. That dependence sounds like a weakness, and often it is. But it comes packaged with an advantage. A spore is a single cell wrapped in a tough coat. It weighs almost nothing, it needs no bee, no bird, and no soil built up over centuries, and the wind will carry it for hundreds of miles. A fern can therefore arrive somewhere no other plant can reach and start from nothing, provided the ground is damp. The rock record shows what that ability is worth. Drill through the layer of clay that marks the asteroid impact of 66 million years ago and the pollen of a forested world vanishes at the boundary. Directly above it, in cores from around the world, comes a flood of fern spores. Paleobotanists call it the fern spike. For years after the sky darkened, much of the ruined landscape was green with almost nothing but ferns. They were not survivors so much as first responders. The second act is stranger, and it runs the other way: instead of the climate rewriting the ferns, the ferns may have rewritten the climate. About 49 million years ago the Earth was hot. The Arctic Ocean was then a nearly enclosed basin, warm and topped with fresh water, and across that surface a tiny floating fern called Azolla bloomed. Azolla grows fast, doubling in a matter of days, partly because it houses bacteria that pull nitrogen straight from the air. Layers of Azolla remains sit in Arctic sediment cores, laid down over roughly 800,000 years. Every one of those plants had pulled carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, and when they sank into a stagnant seafloor, that carbon was buried rather than recycled. Many scientists think this drawdown helped pull the planet out of its hothouse and start the long slide toward the ice ages we live between now. The evidence is circumstantial and the debate is live, but the scale is not in doubt. So the fern's story runs in both directions. Weather dictates where a fern can live, because its sperm must swim. And ferns, given enough time and enough surface, have altered what the weather is. The plant sitting quietly in the shade is not simple. It is patient, and patience at geological scale is a kind of power.
